description: Ungrammatical English sentences the translator must refuse, each with a grammatical control it must accept, so the refusal is grammatical knowledge and not incapacity. Every token is in the lexicon. The source names the published example or the standard rule; adapted means the sentence was changed from the published form (vocabulary, tokenization).

sentences.phenomenon: seem takes an adjective or an infinitive, not a present participle
only an auxiliary inverts with the subject in a question
sentences.source: Chomsky 1957, Syntactic Structures, section 2.3, example (5) 'read you a book on modern music?'

sentences.sentence: what did she buy a book and ?

sentences.source: Ross 1967, Constraints on Variables in Syntax, chapter 4

sentences.phenomenon: at most one modal in the auxiliary
sentences.source: Chomsky 1957, Syntactic Structures, section 7, the auxiliary rule Aux -> C (M) (have+en) (be+ing)

sentences.phenomenon: do-support takes the bare verb; tense is marked once
sentences.source: Chomsky 1957, Syntactic Structures, section 7 (affix hopping and do-support)

sentences.phenomenon: an unaccusative verb has no passive
sentences.source: Perlmutter 1978, Impersonal Passives and the Unaccusative Hypothesis; Burzio 1986, Italian Syntax

sentences.phenomenon: a reflexive needs a c-commanding antecedent and cannot be the subject (Binding Principle A)
sentences.source: Chomsky 1981, Lectures on Government and Binding
